title: The backup-QB game plan: how offenses shrink the playbook (Luke Fahey, Drew Lock, Joe Fagnano)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The original football-film-room repository wasn't reachable (access denied: "not configured for this session"). So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. This lesson adds a new idea, built on this weekend: three backup or first-year QBs in games on the board.

The big idea: a backup QB reads the defense more slowly. So coaches shrink the playbook.Fewer reads per play. More runs. More quick throws. More plays where the QB only looks at half the field.The classic one is the play-action bootleg in the diagram.

White = offense, yellow = defense. A = the fake handoff. B = the QB rolling out to his right ("bootleg"). C = three receivers on the same side at three depths: deep, a 12-yard out, and the flat.

  1. A: the fake. The QB pretends to hand off to the RB running left.The linebacker steps toward the run. That one step opens space behind him. This is play-action.
  2. B: half the field. The QB rolls right, away from the fake. Now he only looks right.The left side is ignored on purpose. Fewer things to read means fewer mistakes. Moving also gets him away from the pass rush.
  3. C: three levels, one easy read. Deep, middle (the out) and short (the flat). It's the three levels from Lesson 44.The QB watches one defender, usually the cornerback. If he sinks with the deep WR, throw the out. If he jumps the out, throw deep. If both are covered, dump it to the TE in the flat.
  4. Real example 1: Joe Fagnano, Thursday. Baltimore's third-string QB threw 18 passes for 60 yards (3.3 an attempt).That's what a very small playbook looks like: short throws, lots of runs, and almost nothing downfield.
  5. Real example 2: Luke Fahey, today. Ohio State's freshman makes his second start against Oregon (12:30 p.m. PT, CBS). In his first, Ohio State lost by 12 at USC.Expect a lot of handoffs, quick throws and a few designed rollouts. That's part of why the total fell to 44.5.
  6. Real example 3: Drew Lock, Sunday. Seattle's backup starts against Arizona (1:25 p.m. PT, FOX) with LT Charles Cross and G Quenton Nelson out.With two linemen missing, moving the pocket with bootlegs is the usual fix. Lock has been good in relief this year: 127.3 rating, 4 TDs, 0 INTs.
  7. The defense's answer. Put an extra defender near the line to stop the run (a loaded box, Lesson 44). Dare the backup to beat you deep.Against a bootleg, the edge rusher must keep contain (Lesson 45): stay outside so the QB can't run around him.

How to use it in your drill: when a backup QB is in, lean Run on 1st down. Watch the QB after the snap: a hard fake and then a sprint to one side is a bootleg. Log it as Pass (play-action). On 3rd and long, expect a quick throw, not a deep drop.

Why it matters for your bets: backup QBs usually mean fewer points, so Unders get popular and totals drop (Market 101, Lesson 44). The risk is turnovers that give the other team short fields (Lesson 46).

Real examples to watch (Pacific time): today, Oregon at Ohio State (12:30 p.m., CBS): count Fahey's rollouts. Sunday, Cardinals at Seahawks (1:25 p.m., FOX): watch Lock's first-quarter play-action.

Video: search YouTube for "play action bootleg explained," "half field read quarterback," and "Ohio State Luke Fahey highlights."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 5: Plays)

quiz.q: Why do coaches shrink the playbook for a backup QB?
o: Backups read defenses more slowly, so fewer reads means fewer mistakes
To save the starter's plays for later
quiz.w: Fewer reads per play, more runs and quick throws, and half-field plays keep a backup out of trouble.

quiz.q: In a play-action bootleg, what does the fake handoff do?
o: Gives the ball to the RB
Makes the linebacker step toward the run, opening space behind him
Moves the QB closer to the line
quiz.w: The linebacker bites on the fake. That step opens a throwing window behind him.

quiz.q: On a bootleg to the right, which side does the QB read?
o: Only the right, half the field
He doesn't read; he always runs
quiz.w: Rolling right cuts the field in half. The left side is ignored on purpose.

quiz.q: In your drill, a backup QB fakes a handoff and sprints to one side. How do you log it?
quiz.w: A hard fake and a rollout is a bootleg: a pass play built off a run fake.
